text: Russia fired about 20,000 artillery rounds a day in Donbas in 2022, with peaks above 32,000.
In 2022 Ukraine rarely fired more than 6,000 artillery rounds a day.
Russia held a 10–12:1 artillery fire advantage over Ukraine by June 2022.

observations.note: Written Russia : Ukraine as 10–12:1; stored as Ukraine : Russia (1:12 to 1:10).

text: HIMARS and M270 GMLRS strikes from late June 2022 broke the Russian artillery model, which depended on railheads and big depots.
RUSI calls the arrival of HIMARS/M270 GMLRS in 2022 "the point where the Russian offensive on Donbas ended".

cites.quote: the point where the Russian offensive on Donbas ended

text: Russian artillery shell use ran short: about 12M rounds were fired in 2022, trending to about 7M in 2023.
In 2023–24 Russia moved to Krasnopol laser-guided shells, Lancet loitering munitions for counter-battery work, and above all mass UMPK glide bombs.
UMPK glide bombs let the VKS (Russian Aerospace Forces) strike the front from 30–90 km without entering Ukrainian SAM coverage.
Russian electronic warfare cut the hit rate of Ukraine's GPS-guided Excalibur shells from more than 50% to 6–7%.
Ukraine rationed artillery shells, and the Ukraine:Russia shell ratio was 1:10 in February 2024.
Tactical UAVs cause 60–70% of damaged and destroyed Russian systems.
Latvian intelligence puts drones at 70–80% of all killed and wounded on both sides by early 2026.
In the drone-dominated kill zone (2024–26), artillery survives by dispersing and digging in, and works as a partner to drones rather than as the main killer.
notes: Uncited synthesis in the overview; cited to the RUSI source the block uses for this regime.

text: The Ukrainian shell ratio recovered to about 1:1.8 (Ukraine:Russia) by July 2025.
The Czech ammunition initiative helped the Ukrainian shell ratio recover by 2025.
Russian KAB glide-bomb use climbed from about 5,000 to almost 8,800 a month during 2026.
Russian Iskander-M output rose to 60–70 missiles a month.
In 2026 Russia launched 100–200 ballistic missiles and up to about 8,000 Shahed/Geran drones a month at Ukraine.
As PAC-3 interceptors ran short in 2026, partly because of the US–Iran war, Ukraine's ballistic-missile intercept rate collapsed to 10–15%.
Ukraine answered Russian deep strikes with its own long-range weapons, above all mass mid-range and long-range drones, plus a small number of Flamingo and Neptune missiles.
notes: Uncited sentence in the overview; tied to the CSIS source the block cites, which covers Ukrainian deep-strike counts.

text: Since early March 2022, Ukrainian ground-based air defence has kept Russian crewed aircraft out of Ukrainian-held airspace except at very low altitude.
Russia's layered IADS confines Ukraine's small air force (MiG-29, Su-27, Su-24M, Su-25, and from 2024–25 F-16 and Mirage 2000) to stand-off strikes and anti-missile and anti-drone patrols.
notes: Uncited synthesis; tied to the block's RUSI air-war source.

text: Neither Russia nor Ukraine has air superiority; the air war stayed contested.
Glide bombs are Russia's workaround for the lack of air superiority: RUSI writes that "Glide bombs gave the VKS teeth without the need to first achieve air superiority".

cites.quote: Glide bombs gave the VKS teeth without the need to first achieve air superiority

text: About 75% of static Ukrainian SAM sites were engaged by Russian strikes in the first 48 h of the February 2022 invasion.

observations.subject: static Ukrainian SAM sites engaged in the first 48 h

text: Mobile Ukrainian air-defence systems survived the opening Russian strike campaign in 2022 through dispersal and deception: dummy sites, printed "damage" sheets over hangars, and false radio reports of destroyed sites.
Russian battle damage assessment (BDA) was weak during the opening strike campaign of 2022.
From early March 2022 the VKS lost the ability to operate over Ukrainian-held territory except at very low altitude.
Pre-war Ukrainian air defence had 35 S-300PS/PT divisions, 3 S-300V, 9 S-125 and 15 Buk-M1, with MANPADS (mostly modernised Igla-1) spread through units.
notes: Source text gives unit counts for S-300V, S-125 and Buk-M1 without a unit; likely also divisions.

text: In 2022 Ukrainian SAMs forced Russian aircraft down low, into the MANPADS envelope.
Russia made more than 200 Iskander strikes and about 180 Kh-22/32 and Kh-55/555 launches from February to early May 2022.
By early April 2022 Russia had moved from missile salvos to single shots, probably because of stock shortages.
Russian Iskander-M output was estimated at about 6 missiles a month in 2022.
Short of Iskanders in spring 2022, Russia fell back on Tochka-U, Bal and Bastion missiles, with more civilian damage as a result.
Russian air-assault helicopters reached Hostomel flying low along the Dnipro in February 2022, but MANPADS downed 2 in the first wave.

observations.subject: Russian helicopters downed by MANPADS in the first wave

observations.subject: Oryx-confirmed helicopter losses (4 Ka-52, 1 Mi-28, 1 Mi-8)

text: Ukrainian helicopter lob-fire salvos force infantry to take cover but rarely kill armour or dug-in positions.
In early 2022 Ukrainian Su-24M, Su-25, Mi-24 and Mi-8 struck Russian convoys that were moving without air cover.
In 2022 Ukrainian MiG-29 pairs flew defensive counter-air, often outnumbered 6:2.

observations.subject: Russian to Ukrainian aircraft in air engagements

text: In 2022 Ukraine deconflicted its airspace from its own SAMs first by time, then by area.
In 2022 Russia relied on pre-planned strikes and presumed success.
Ukraine's pre-war Kropyva digital fire-control software had cut the time to open counter-battery fire by 90% and the time to engage unplanned targets by two-thirds.
In May–August 2022 Russia averaged about 20,000 artillery rounds a day, peaking above 32,000.
In May–June 2022 Russia had more than 1,100 tube guns in Donbas, in groups of 80–90 per brigade-sized grouping, giving a 12:1 artillery advantage.

In 2022 Russia used Uragan and Smerch MLRS at maximum range (35–70 km), even against point targets.

text: The Orlan-10 stood out among Russian artillery-spotting UAVs in 2022.
From late June 2022, HIMARS GMLRS systematically hit Russian depots that had been mapped from Russian dependence on rail; RUSI marks this as the end of the Russian Donbas offensive.
After the July 2022 HIMARS strikes on C2 and depots, Russia could no longer stockpile ammunition beside its guns.
After the 2022 HIMARS strikes, Russia could no longer mass ammunition beside its guns and had to haul it from depots further back.

Over-stretched Russian artillery logistics after the HIMARS strikes is the backdrop to Ukraine's autumn 2022 Kharkiv and Kherson offensives (research-file inference, not a direct claim of the source).
In autumn 2022 Russia began sending hundreds of Iranian Shahed-136 drones against Ukrainian substations, together with cruise and ballistic missiles.
RUSI urged more MANPADS, radar-guided AA guns and Western fighters as affordable counters to the 2022 Shahed campaign.
In Q1 2023 Russia fired 12,000–38,000 artillery rounds a day, and days above 24,000 became rare.
In early 2023 Russian artillery use shifted from 152 mm guns to 120 mm mortars.
Russia's annual artillery consumption was trending to about 7M rounds in 2023, against Ukrainian estimates of about 2.5M rounds a year in Russian production.
In 2023 each Russian axis commander kept Orlan-10 orbits overhead, and the artillery brigade flew its own UAV complex, in what Russia calls the reconnaissance-fire circuit.
In 2023 Russian artillery engaged about 3–5 min after UAV detection and 20–30 min after EW detection.
The Russian Strelets system links sensors to digital fire control.
In 2023 Russian Krasnopol laser-guided shells and Lancet loitering munitions did counter-battery work and hunted Ukrainian guns.
By early 2023 Russian air defence was intercepting a share of GMLRS rockets.
Excalibur's confirmed hit rate fell from more than 55% early in 2023 to 7% in July and 6% in August 2023.
JDAM-ER glide-bomb kits, delivered to Ukraine from February 2023, lost accuracy within weeks, and a patch followed in May 2023.
In early 2023 the VKS stayed stand-off, using FAB-500s with early glide kits from Su-35S out to about 70 km, in small but steady numbers, plus lofted S-8 rockets.
In early 2023 Russian industry supplied about 40 long-range missiles a month.
Russian Tu-95 strike packages used Shaheds as pathfinders to find gaps in Ukrainian air defence.
In the 2023 counteroffensive, Ukrainian M777 batteries normally had to displace 2–15 min after opening fire.

metric_new.label: Gun displacement time after opening fire

text: Ammunition hoarded for the 2023 Ukrainian offensive allowed a short "freedom to fire".
In 2023 the Ka-52 firing Vikhr and Ataka ATGMs was the leading Russian aviation threat, and Mi-35M added Ataka and lofted S-8 salvos.
In 2023 Russian attack-helicopter strikes came from 8–10 km, often with an EW-escort helicopter.
Ukrainian troops learned in 2023 that when Russian GPS jamming lifted, attack helicopters were coming.
Around Robotyne in 2023 the UK MoD called the Ka-52 "one of the most influential Russian weapons systems" against the Ukrainian offensive.

cites.quote: one of the most influential Russian weapons systems

text: In 2023 the Ka-52 flew at 50–100 m and carried up to 12 Vikhr ATGMs with about 8 km range.

text: Oryx has 69 Russian Ka-52 losses confirmed over the whole war.

text: Glide bombs were already a significant factor on the Zaporizhzhia front in summer 2023.
Storm Shadow, fired from Ukrainian Su-24M since May 2023, hit the Chonhar bridges and, on 22 Sep 2023, the Black Sea Fleet HQ in Sevastopol.
The first Ukrainian ATACMS strikes, in October 2023, destroyed helicopters on occupied airfields.
The GBU-39 small-diameter bomb, delivered to Ukraine from November 2023, hit about 90% of the time.
The Ukraine:Russia shell ratio reached 1:10 in February 2024 while US aid was stalled.

text: Ukraine received about 1.6M 155 mm shells in 2023 and 1.5M in 2024.
By 2024–25 Ukrainian brigades had shells but lacked charges and spares, and could rarely get DPICM or BONUS rounds.
Tactical UAVs account for 60–70% of damaged or destroyed Russian systems, even though 60–80% of FPVs fail to reach the target.

text: In 2024–25 both sides spaced guns more than 500 m apart, dug them in with overhead cover, and used hides with clusters of firing positions and decoys.
In 2024–25 guns moved mainly to escape glide bombs.
Russian glide bombs are released 30–90 km from the target, and Ukraine had "no effective countermeasures" as of 2024–25.
About 50% of Ukrainian casualties are taken in the rear, from FPVs, artillery and glide bombs.

observations.subject: Ukrainian casualties taken in the rear

text: Forward-pushed Ukrainian SAMs get found and killed with 9M723 Iskander missiles.
Helicopters and fighter CAPs are the most efficient killers of high-flying Gerans, with mobile fire groups, AA guns and MANPADS as point defence.
Syrskyi says Mi-8 and Mi-24 crews with machine guns downed more than 3,200 Shahed-type drones between August 2024 and August 2025.
Ukrainian interceptor UAVs are thinning out Russian Orlan and Zala reconnaissance drones.
In October 2024 Russia launched 1,900 Shaheds, 33 ballistic and 42 cruise missiles at Ukraine.

text: After HIMARS, barrel wear and shell shortages, Russia judged massed norm-based fire "non-viable" and moved to the reconnaissance-fire complex (Orlan-10 plus Strelets plus Krasnopol and Lancet), prioritising effect over volume.
The VKS lost the struggle to suppress Ukrainian air defence in March 2022.
After March 2022 the VKS fell back on stand-off munitions: cruise missiles from Tu-95/Tu-160, lofted S-8, and then glide bombs, acting as a "force in being".
The glide bomb turned a latent Russian air force into the main source of heavy firepower at the front.
Russian UMPK production went from tens of thousands to more than 100,000 a year.
Russian Iskander-M output rose tenfold from 2022 to 2025.

text: Russian Shahed/Geran output supports waves of thousands a month.
CSIS reads the Russian strike rhythm as "industrial rhythm more than battlefield design".

text: Russia makes up shell shortfalls with North Korean ammunition, launchers and KN-23 missiles.
HUR counts more than 7M North Korean artillery rounds, 600+ guns and 100+ KN-23/KN-24 delivered to Russia since June 2023.

text: By 2026 Russian KAB use (283 a day in August 2026) exceeds the US bombing rate over Iran.
Russian strike missiles are routed around Ukrainian EW and SAM positions and arrive from several directions at once; Iskander carries decoys and the Kh-101 has better terminal guidance and flares.
Russian drone waves map Ukrainian air defence and drain its interceptors.
In 2026 Russia pairs jet Gerans with ballistic salvos to exploit the Patriot shortage.
Russian KABs support infantry directly, as at Avdiivka.
Russian KABs cut bridges and roads in the Ukrainian rear, as with FAB-3000 on the H-20 highway in February 2026.
Russian KABs reduce near-rear towns to ruins that Russian infiltrators then use as cover.
Russian artillery brigades and regiments field their own drone operators.
Russian rocket minelayers (Zemledeliye, 5–15 km) seed minefields across breach lanes and supply routes.
Newer Russian tools include extended-range and powered glide bombs.
Newer Russian tools include jet Gerans, among them the air-launched Geran-5 with optional R-73 missiles.
Russia uses the Oreshnik IRBM as a signalling weapon.
Russian vulnerabilities included rail and depot dependence (2022) and exposed forward arming and refuelling points for helicopters close to the front (2023).
Until February 2026 Russian forces depended on Starlink and Telegram for drone feeds and coordinates, a vulnerability.
Russian missile plants such as Votkinsk are within reach of the Flamingo.
Russia's air-defence network, thinned by Ukraine's SEAD campaign, exposes GLOCs 100–160 km deep.

rationale: The Ukrainian domestic glide bomb may carry CRPA anti-jam antennas, the standard answer to GNSS jamming that degraded Excalibur and JDAM-ER.
Russian jamming cut Excalibur's hit rate from more than 50–55% to 6–7% in 2023.
JDAM-ER lost accuracy within weeks of delivery; jamming caused misses of up to about 1 km.
GMLRS was later degraded by Russian EW; up to 10 EW complexes per 20 km degraded Ukrainian precision fires.
By 2023 Russian air defence intercepted a share of GMLRS.

effect: forced ammunition back to rear depots
rationale: GMLRS hit depots mapped from Russian rail dependence, and Russia could no longer stockpile ammunition beside its guns.
Glide bombs released 30–90 km out let the VKS strike without entering Ukrainian SAM coverage.

effect: up to ~100 intercepted in three months
rationale: Ukrainian SAM units killed up to 100 KABs in September–November 2025, the first real anti-KAB capability.
Pokrova jamming degrades KAB accuracy.
Interceptor drones took a growing share of Shahed kills from late 2025, about 50% by May 2026, at about $2,000 against a $20–50k target.
At about 500 km/h, jet Gerans are beyond current interceptor drones.

effect: mobile fire groups no longer reliable
rationale: Jet Gerans complicate the work of mobile fire groups, which Ihnat says can no longer be relied on against them.
Mi-8 and Mi-24 crews downed more than 3,200 Shahed-type drones in Aug 2024–Aug 2025 and take up to 40% in their zones.
A Shahed carrying an R-60 air-to-air missile aimed at helicopters appeared in December 2025.
MANPADS downed 2 helicopters in the first wave at Hostomel, and the 47th Brigade downed Ka-52s near Robotyne.
Pitch-up lob firing of S-8 gains 6–7 km and keeps the helicopter out of Stinger range, at the cost of dispersion.
The LMUR's ~15 km range is well beyond the ~6 km reach of a Stinger.
Forward-pushed Ukrainian SAMs get found and killed with 9M723 Iskander.
Interceptor UAVs are thinning out Russian Orlan and Zala reconnaissance drones.
Kh-101 upgrades include flares against MANPADS.

effect: only effective ABM; 2–3 interceptors per missile
rationale: Patriot and SAMP/T are the only Ukrainian systems able to intercept Iskander, at 2–3 interceptors per missile.
Russian missiles are routed around EW and SAM positions and arrive from several directions; Iskander carries decoys.
Russian drone waves (35–40% decoys) map Ukrainian air defence and drain its interceptors.

counter: Gun dispersal, dig-in and decoy hides
rationale: Both sides space guns more than 500 m apart, dig in with overhead cover and use decoys; guns move mainly to escape glide bombs.

counter: SAM dispersal, dummy sites and deception
measure: Russian opening strike campaign against air defence
effect: air defence survived the opening strikes
rationale: Mobile SAMs survived the opening strikes through dispersal, dummy sites and false reports, while Russian BDA was weak.

measure: Russian drone-feed relay over Starlink and Telegram
rationale: Losing Starlink and Telegram made the Russian sensor-to-shooter chain less efficient without collapsing C2.

effect: opened airspace, exposed GLOCs 100–160 km deep
rationale: Oryx confirms 77 Russian SAMs and 23 radars destroyed in 2025, and the SEAD campaign opened Russian-held airspace.
FPVs have hit both Ka-52 and Mi-28 helicopters.

counter: Mobile fire groups, AA guns and MANPADS
rationale: Mobile fire groups, AA guns and MANPADS act as point defence against Gerans, wearing down waves en route.
Helicopters and fighter CAPs are the most efficient killers of high-flying Gerans.
